newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - Direct injection petrol engines, wrinkle or revolution.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Direct injection petrol engines, wrinkle or revolution.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
The diesel's shaky reign as the car's most environmentally friendly engine could soon be over.
Mitsubishi Motors has launched the direct injection petrol engine in Japan, and will introduce it in Europe late next year.
The Japanese company says its new engine can match the diesel for economy while still retaining the petrol engine's overwhelming superiority in performance produced with smoothness.
Toyota Motor Corp is launching a similar power plant later this year.
All the world's major car makers are said to be working on similar engines.
Direct injection engines have enhanced performance mainly because of technology which can squirt a precise amount of fuel and air straight into the combustion chamber.
Pollution problems are said to be negligible and the new engine will have no particulate emissions -- the minute, unburnt and possibly carcinogenic molecules of fuel released by diesel engines.

Diesel-powered cars have become increasingly popular in Europe, especially France, where around 45 percent of new cars are diesels. The surge in sales of these economical, but often rattling and smoky engines, has been partly tax driven, coupled with a huge advantage in fuel economy.
Modern diesels are cleaner and smoother than before, but even their most ardent admirers can't shake the worry over particulates.

"The direct injection petrol engine is almost as efficient as the diesel and, if they can make it reliable, the diesel people would have a big problem," said Professor Douglas Greenhalgh of Britain's Cranfield University.
Mitsubishi, which is launching the new engine in 1.8 litre 4-cylinder version of its Galant family car, has an array of claims for the system.
- 35 percent improvement in fuel economy in town driving.
- Eight percent better than conventional engines at 75 miles (120 km) per hour.
- 40 percent better at idling speeds. The technology allows lower idling at 600 revolutions per minute, compared with 750.

Mitsubishi says the direct injection technology allows a very lean air-to-fuel ratio of 40 to one, compared with the conventional 15 to one, giving 10 percent improvement in power over current engines of the same size.
Mitsubishi's Kiyotaka Takizawa told journalists at this week's Paris Car Show that this engine will become the standard power plant for cars in the 21st century.

"Over a diesel engine of a comparable capacity the new technology Mitsubishi engine yields about seven percent better fuel economy, 85 percent more power...zero particulate emissions ...lower noise levels at all speeds, eight percent lighter in weight and 40 percent lower production costs," Takizawa said.
The direct injection petrol engine is not a new idea. About 10 years ago, German mass car maker Volkswagen said its engineers had produced one, but it never found its way on to the showroom floor.
VW could reproduce all the advantages in efficiency, but was unable to overcome the problem of reliability.
Mitsubishi says that a combination of advances provided by expertise in the Mitubishi group of companies was behind the breakthrough.

Much of it was due to advanced computer-powered engine management which gives the split second precision to inject just the right combination of air and fuel at the right moment. Fuel injection technology solved the problem of lubrication.
But there have been many different power plants over the years which were about to overwhelm the traditional internal combustion petrol engine's faltering dominance.

"If they invented it (the internal comubustion engine) today, it's so grossly inefficient, they would have thrown it on the scrapheap straightaway. But they've been improved over the years and there must be over a billion of them around the world today," said Dr David Wood from Durham University's advanced automobile engineering school in northeast England.

The orbital engine and the rotary engine had their five minutes of fame as contenders before fading away. Battery power has almost been the answer to the need for clean, efficient power for almost 100 years.
The hydrogen engine is said to have the inside track in providing non-polluting traction with no environmental drawbacks, but not for about 20 years.
The diesel has been refined over the years to give it more power and reform its dirty, noisy image. Some experts say this is still the way to go.

"The direct injection engine sounds wonderful, but remember the Ford Ka (the new minicar unveiled here this week) was supposed to be powered by the Orbital engine," said Peter Schmidt, analyst at Britain's Automotive Industry Data consultancy.

"You brush aside diesel at your peril. The technology is proven, its got a long track record -- in Germany every Mercedes taxi driver will show you how mature they are. Diesels have been vastly improved for refinement, power, fuel economy and emissions. But, yes, there is the particulate problem," Schmidt said.
Joe Gormezano, from British automotive industry consultants Knibb Gormezano, is impressed by the direct injection engine, but sees more radical changes in future automobile use.

"I don't think direct injection petrol is just a wrinkle, it's very serious, depending to what extent the need for fuel economy is taken seriously. There's every indication this is the case in Japan and Europe, but the U.S. is not interested in fuel economy," Gormezano said.
He sees more alternative fuels emerging as the industry seeks more fuel efficiency and cleanliness.
Hybrids, which use a combination of fossil fuel and battery power, are favoured by Gormezano.
Durham University's Wood expects the family of the future to have two cars, given the fact that battery power is never likely to be able to compete in range and power with petrol and diesel engines.

One car will be a battery powered little vehicle to do the shopping. The fact that it will have no great range will be immaterial. It would be allowed into city centres. The second car would be used for greater distances and would be banned from cities.
The world's big automotive companies will be monitoring the performace of Mitsubishi's new direct injection with care and perhaps alarm.
If it matches the hype, engineers at other big car makers will be working late for the foreseable future as they scramble to match a winning product.
